1.pericope_label: Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim... And the glorious beauty, which is on the head of the fat valley, shall be a fading flower, and as the hasty fruit before the summer

schools.summary: Delitzsch dates the chapter to Hezekiah's earliest years, since Samaria has not yet fallen, and sets the chapters that follow against the preceding ones as a mirror of two reigns, the earlier marked by spiritless submission to the Assyrian yoke, this one by a striving after liberty in reliance on Egypt rather than on God; he also renders the mighty one of the second verse in the neuter, a strong and mighty thing held ready like a hailstorm. Ellicott finds the chapter remarkable because the prophet's work here reaches the northern kingdom rather than Judah alone, dates the warning before the capital fell, and sees a bold personification working twice, first the banquet with its flower-wreathed revellers and then Samaria itself as such a wreath, once beautiful and now fading; on the disputed phrase he allows the Hebrew to be neuter or masculine and says either way it points to the Assyrian king, and on the fig he takes the earliest crop as a type of the doomed city's pride, seized and devoured by the passer-by with a homeliness he calls worthy of Dante.

Gill distinguishes being cast down by the hand from being trampled by the feet, the one showing destruction and the other contempt. Calvin marks the chapter off as a new subject, the vengeance of God falling first on Israel and afterwards on the Jews; he prefers to take the mighty one without a substantive, as a staff or other instrument by which the Lord will cast down this pride, keeping the flower of the opening verse in view since nothing is more destructive to flowers than hail; and he explains the near-repetition of the fourth verse by the difficulty of terrifying men blinded by prosperity, adding the example of a tyrant so gorged at unseasonable banquets that he stumbled constantly.

Clarke lays out the chapter's plan, a denunciation of the northern ruin, a turn to the two tribes who were to continue after their brethren's captivity, and then reproofs for intemperance and profaneness; he construes the disputed phrase as a Hebraism for the exceedingly strong one, reports that many manuscripts read the divine name where our text has Lord, would read crowns in the plural to agree with its verb, and quotes a traveller on the fig tree's three crops, the last of which ripens after the leaves are shed and is gathered as a delicious morsel in spring. Wesley gives the kingdom in short, a proud one whose many excellent vines exposed it to the sin charged against it, and draws out the force of the verb, that the crown on their own heads shall be trodden under the feet of others and men whose drunkenness had brought them to the ground shall be trodden down there.

Henry supplies the setting: Ephraim took his name from fruitfulness, and Samaria, seated on a hill, stood as on the head of the fat valleys, the country pleasant as the garden of the Lord and its harvest and vintage the glorious beauty.

debates.question: Is the mighty and strong one a person or a thing?

positions.view: A thing: the phrase is neuter, a strong and mighty thing like a hailstorm.
Neuter or masculine, but either way the Assyrian king as God's instrument.
Better taken without a substantive at all, as a staff or other instrument.
The Assyrian king, named outright.
A Hebraism for the exceedingly strong one.

debates.question: What does the crown of pride stand for?

positions.view: Samaria itself, personified as a fading flower-wreath on the head of the luxuriant valley.
The rich country and its capital, the harvest and vintage being the glorious beauty.
A proud kingdom whose vines exposed it to drunkenness, its crown to be trodden underfoot by others.

outliers.note: Departs into natural history, quoting a traveller on the fig tree's three annual crops down to the winter fig gathered in spring.
Uses the chapter to date a whole block of the book, reading the following chapters as a mirror of Hezekiah's reign against the preceding ones as a mirror of Ahaz's.

themes: Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, whose glorious beauty is a fading flower, which are on the head of the fat valleys of them that are overcome with wine!
Behold, the Lord hath a mighty and strong one, which as a tempest of hail and a destroying storm, as a flood of mighty waters overflowing, shall cast down to the earth with the hand.
The crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim, shall be trodden under feet:

And the glorious beauty, which is on the head of the fat valley, shall be a fading flower, and as the hasty fruit before the summer; which when he that looketh upon it seeth, while it is yet in his hand he eateth it up.

5.pericope_label: In that day shall the LORD of hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty, unto the residue of his people... For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the crown of glory in direct contrast with the crown of pride just trampled, finds an earnest of the promise in the gathering of some northern tribes at the king's passover, hears an echo of the spiritual gifts listed earlier in the book, and notes that corrupt judges were the crying evil of both capitals, taking the brave men set beside the upright judges as those who drive the enemy back to the gate he came out of. On the reproof he hears the method of the prophet who said thou art the man: having painted the drunkards of one capital, the prophet paints those of the other in darker colours still, priests reeling to their services and prophets reeling in the very act of their counterfeit inspiration, the word for reeling repeated three times to press the scandal home. Delitzsch notes that with the words and they also the prophet opens the address's second half and passes from the northern kingdom to Judah, and carries the scene into the sneer that follows, the hearers treating him as an intolerable moralist and answering that they are of age and free.

Gill takes the crown as surrounding and protecting a people to whom God gives large measures of grace, and dates it to the year the ten tribes were carried away; he applies the spirit of judgment to the king, or, with a rabbinic reading, to the whole council of judges; and on the fouled tables he distinguishes the two words, one for what a loaded stomach throws up and the other for what the body voids, noting that the tables meant are those of the priests who ate the holy things and of the prophets who pretended to see visions. Calvin will not extend the promise indiscriminately to all the Jews but only to the elect wonderfully rescued from death, and draws the rule that the Church is never so disfigured that the Lord does not adorn it; he says the art of civil government consists of counsel within and strength against enemies without, and that God gives both; he takes the wine and strong drink metaphorically and reads a charge of aggravated ingratitude, since these men had a striking proof of God's anger in their brethren's chastisement while experiencing his forbearance toward themselves; and he draws the moral that men given to drunkenness forget shame and shrink from nothing disgraceful.

Clarke says the prophecy has so far related to the Israelites and now turns to the two tribes, opening with a favourable prognostication that soon changes to reproof; he reports that the ancient Aramaic paraphrase read the verse of the Messiah outright, and prefers to render the following clause as the war carried to the enemy's own gate. Wesley says Judah is guilty of the same sins and must expect the same calamities, the prophets miscarrying in their sacred employment while the priests mistake in pronouncing the sentence of the law.
Henry narrows the promise to those who glory in the Lord of hosts himself, adding that only in Christ does a holy God communicate with sinful man.

debates.question: Who receives the crown of glory?

positions.view: The remnant of Israel as well as of Judah, whose union the king's passover had already foreshadowed.
Only the elect, not all the Jews indiscriminately.
Those who glory in the Lord of hosts himself.
The people of Judah, at the time the ten tribes were carried away.

debates.question: Is the drunkenness of the priests and prophets literal?

positions.view: Literal, and a vice common to every rank.
Metaphorical: the charge is aggravated ingratitude, not intoxication.

outliers.note: Reports the Targum reading both the crown of glory and the victory at the gate directly of the Messiah, and thinks the paraphrase worthy of notice.

themes: In that day shall the Lord of hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty, unto the residue of his people,
And for a spirit of judgment to him that sitteth in judgment, and for strength to them that turn the battle to the gate.

But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, they are out of the way through strong drink; they err in vision, they stumble in judgment.
For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean.

9.pericope_label: Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine?... But the word of the LORD was unto them precept upon precept, line upon line; here a little, and there a little

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the opening verses as the drunkards talking scornfully of a man who comes to them with what he calls his knowledge as though they were boys fit for an infant school, the iteration they ascribe to him being puerile harping on one note, and can scarcely doubt the prophet was reproducing their words; he makes the stammering lips those of the Assyrian conquerors, whose speech would strike the men of Judah as a barbarous patois and who would next utter God's will to a people that would not hear the prophet; and he has the prophet vindicate himself against the charge of endlessly repeating rebuke, since he had pointed the way to repentance and so to rest, repeating their one formula of derision back at them with all the scorn of irony. Delitzsch takes the connecting word out of the scoffers' mouths and carries it on in the prophet's, ungodliness of that kind meeting an appropriate punishment.

Gill asks whom such a teacher can instruct in the knowledge of God and the way of salvation, and will have the stammering either way, as the lisping by which parents accommodate a child's weakness or as the rougher speech of an invading people. Calvin turns the first verse into amazement that the disease is incurable, since calling wanderers back and unceasingly warning those who stray is itself an extraordinary remedy; he makes the repeated formula a schoolroom where the master spends a whole day on a single letter and must renew the labour next day; he refers the stammering to God himself, who became a barbarian to a people without understanding, so that by their own fault they made the God who formed our tongues appear a stammerer; and he rejects as feeble the reading that turns the offer of rest into a supposition, holding that the prophet is giving the reason why God seemed to them a barbarian, which is that they had no ears.

Clarke has the scoffers uttering their own sententious speeches and treating God's warnings with derision, their mockery ridiculing the prophet's own concise manner before God retorts with great severity; he calls the original remarkably abrupt and explains its two nouns, the first a diminutive suited to a child's capacity and used so nowhere else, the second the mason's line stretched to build a course of stones by and raised again for each layer. Wesley reduces the first verse to a sentence, that a minister may as soon teach an infant as these men, says the same of the stammering as Ellicott, a people of strange language brought among them because they would not hear God in their own, and makes the rest the doctrine itself, the only way in which they would find any.

Henry complains of the wretched stupidity of a people unteachable and making no improvement of the means of grace they had, since it is God's way to enlighten the mind with his truth and so gain the affections.

debates.question: Whose words are precept upon precept, line upon line?

positions.view: The scoffers', mocking and imitating the prophet's own concise manner.
The prophet's, describing how such a people has to be taught, like children over a single letter.
The Assyrian conquerors', a barbarous patois with short sharp commands.
God's own, made to seem a stammerer by their fault.
Either a nurse's lisping or a foreign invader's speech.
An appropriate punishment, the prophet turning their own word back on them.

outliers.note: Refers the stammering to God rather than to any human speaker, so that the people's own dullness turns the maker of tongues into a barbarian.

themes: Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them that are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts.
For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:
For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people.
To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear.

But the word of the Lord was unto them precept upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little; that they might go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.

14.pericope_label: Wherefore hear the word of the LORD, ye scornful men, that rule this people which is in Jerusalem... Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the men who derided the prophet among the king's own princes and counsellors, partisans now of an Assyrian and now of an Egyptian alliance, anything rather than a policy of righteousness; he agrees the covenant with death was a proverbial phrase, notes that the second term is the Hebrew word for the region of the dead, and hears in the clause about the overflowing scourge a sneer at the prophet's own imagery, since he had painted the invasion first as a flood and then as a scourge. On the stone he separates two questions usually run together: first the imagery, ancient architecture attaching the same importance to a foundation stone that modern does, with that stone in Zion laid on the solid rock; then the interpretation, which from the prophet's own standpoint was identical with the manifestation of God's righteousness in and through the temple. Delitzsch sets the verses out as one movement.

Gill has them thinking the boast rather than saying it, their conduct showing the sentiments of their minds, and explains why the promise of the stone stands in the middle of a denunciation: the godly, hearing the sentence, might conclude the nation was to be cut off and the house of David ended, and then ask where the promise of the Messiah was. Calvin defines the name of scorners as men addicted to sophistry and deceit who suppose that by jeers and cunning they can escape God's judgment, and notes that the address is not to ordinary men but to rulers who thought they surpassed everyone else in sharpness; he says they promised themselves escape in the middle of their crimes and grew bolder for it; and he takes the comfort of the stone rather than its identification, since the godly were a laughingstock to these crafty men, as irreligious men still reckon believers fools for hoping amid deep adversity that things will turn out well.

Clarke explains that to be in covenant with a thing was a common way of saying one was safe from it, and finds a close parallel in the Roman poet's account of a tribe unhurt by serpents; on the stone he reports that one rabbi understood the verse of the king then reigning, but says it belongs to Jesus Christ alone, and that even the Jews could not contest his application of it to himself. Wesley makes the lying and dissimulation itself their security, works through the epithets of the stone as the Messiah, tried and approved as every way sufficient and uniting the parts of the building, and draws the practical edge from the last clause, that the man who believes will not hastily catch at any way of escaping danger but will wait patiently upon God.

Henry marks the escalation, that having reproved those who made a jest of the word of God the prophet turns on those who made a jest of his judgments, and observes how bad it is with a people when the thrones of judgment become the seats of the scornful; he calls the stone a promise of Christ as the only foundation of hope for escaping the wrath to come, laid in Zion in the eternal counsels of God, a tried stone that never failed anyone who made trial of it.

debates.question: Who or what is the tried stone laid in Zion?

positions.view: Jesus Christ alone, against the rabbinic reading that made it the reigning king.
Christ, the only foundation of hope for escaping the wrath to come.
The Messiah promised, whose promise the sentence of judgment seemed to threaten.
From the prophet's own standpoint, the manifestation of God's righteousness in and through the temple.
The ground of the godly's hope, taken as comfort rather than identified with a person.

debates.question: What is the covenant with death?

positions.view: A proverbial way of claiming perfect safety, paralleled in classical and scriptural writers.
A proverb sharpened into a sneer at the prophet's own images of flood and scourge.
A promise of impunity made to themselves by men who ridiculed all God's threatenings.
A security they expected from lying and dissimulation.

outliers.note: Insists on separating the imagery of the foundation stone from its interpretation, and stops the interpretation at the temple rather than carrying it to a person.

themes: Wherefore hear the word of the Lord, ye scornful men, that rule this people which is in Jerusalem.

Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
Therefore thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.

17.pericope_label: Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet... Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the clause that judgment is made a line and righteousness a plummet, continues the architecture in the elect corner stone that comes up to the standard of perfection, and has the scorners' shelter swept away by the great waters; he brings the dread rumours of the Assyrian march day by day, so that the report which had been unintelligible becomes plain and mourning replaces line upon line, applies the proverb of the bed to the Egyptian alliance the counsellors had made and must lie on, and points out that at both battles named God had interposed for his people, so that the new and strange thing, the very paradox of prophecy, is that he should now rise up to overthrow them. Delitzsch observes that repentance was still possible and at least a modification of the threat attainable, the assumption being that they are already in fetters which their mockery would only make stronger.

Gill notes that the term for disannulled properly means besmeared or daubed over, the word used of the pitching of the ark, so the covenant is blotted like writing spoiled by ink until its articles cannot be made out; he recalls that the Lord broke forth on David's enemies as a breach of waters, whence the place got its name; and he remarks how natural mockery is when judgment is deferred, and that it was one cause of the ruin that came. Calvin reads the line and plummet as a promise that God has the means ready to form the Church anew, though the words indirectly reprove men who wished to be counted pillars of that Church while pulling it down; he explains the state of mind the scourge interrupts, wicked men perceiving they are liable to calamities but stupefying themselves with proverbs about not distressing oneself before the time; and he makes the short bed torture rather than discomfort, the thing given for rest becoming an instrument of pain.

Clarke thinks the word for disannulled does not belong here and prefers the Chaldee's reading, approved by two scholars; on the proverb of the bed he says it means that every means of defence will prove insufficient, notes that the word for covering serves elsewhere for the outworks that form a country's barrier, and describes the furniture, beds being mattresses on the floor and the coverlet a sheet or in winter a carpet a man wrapped himself in. Wesley turns the builder's tools the other way, since a plumb-line serves not only in raising a building but in taking one down and marking the parts to be demolished; and he says the scourge will not merely come but abide, returning morning after morning without the least respite, so dreadful that the rumour alone strikes horror.

debates.question: Do the line and plummet build or demolish?

positions.view: Build: the elect corner stone comes up to the standard, and the false refuge is swept away.
Build: God has the means ready to form the Church entirely anew.
Demolish: the plumb-line marks out the parts of a building that are to come down.
That at the battles named God had risen for his people, and now rises to overthrow them.
That the covenant is not annulled but blotted out like spoiled writing, at the place where God once broke forth for David.
That the bed given for rest becomes an instrument of torture.

outliers.note: Reads the closing warning as leaving a door open, since repentance was still possible and at least a modification of the threat attainable.
Rejects the received word for disannulled outright in favour of the Chaldee's, and glosses the covering of the proverb by the outworks that form a country's barrier.

themes: Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.
And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it.
From the time that it goeth forth it shall take you: for morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night: and it shall be a vexation only to understand the report.
For the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it.
For the Lord shall rise up as in mount Perazim, he shall be wroth as in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his work, his strange work; and bring to pass his act, his strange act.
Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong: for I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consumption, even determined upon the whole earth.

23.pericope_label: Give ye ear, and hear my voice; hearken, and hear my speech... This also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working

schools.summary: Delitzsch says an ingredient is still wanting to balance the first half, since the prophet must comfort the believers who make themselves his disciples as well as alarm the scoffers. Ellicott notes that the parable is set before them uninterpreted, and finds its root idea in men's failure to bring to the signs of the times the wisdom they use readily in tillage; he makes the ploughing the preparatory discipline that fits the spiritual soil for the sower, a means and not an end and so only for a season, which to a nation watching Assyrian invaders score their furrows across the land held out hope of a harvest; he calls the sowing an excerpt from the Georgics of Palestine and follows a modern scholar in reading fennel seed where our version gives fitches; he makes the tiller's skill nothing less than a gift of God, where Gentile legends wrapped the same truth in myths; and he turns the last verse into a question, answering that Israel in its greatness was the bread corn needing a severer threshing, but that the end of threshing is to preserve the true grain and the wheels stop when their work is done.

Gill says the ploughman ploughs in order to sow and may plough a whole day but not every day, the Lord likewise not being always at one task. Calvin observes the mismatch between so weighty a preface and so ordinary a subject and says the prophet meant to lift his hearers higher, showing with what wisdom God governs a world wicked men think moves by chance; he sets himself against the received reading of the parable, which explains it as a reproach for ingratitude, God having cultivated the field and reaped nothing worth having, and connects it instead with what had been said of the destruction revealed to him, that God does not always display his hand in one way; he has the sower measure the ground rather than throw in all he can and takes the disputed word to mean in measure; and he presses an argument from the less to the greater, that if men are so well taught in small matters the teacher himself must know when to cut down a people and what chastisement suits each.

Clarke has the prophet close a discourse of severe reproof with a defence of God's method, in an allegory drawn wholly from agriculture; he distinguishes four threshing instruments, the flail for tenderer grain, the drag of rough planks studded with stones and drawn over the sheaves, the wheeled wain, and the treading of cattle; and he closes on the text, restoring a conjunction on two versions' authority and reading hoofs for horsemen, words that differ by a single letter. Wesley draws the rebuke from the ploughing, that God has his times and seasons and the scoffers flattered themselves foolishly on his long patience, since he will take a time to thresh them, and keeps the plainer sense of the sowing, the best grain chosen for seed, each kind in its place.
Henry compares the parable to those of the Gospels and keeps the plain sense, the husbandman going about his calling with pains and prudence.

debates.question: What is the parable of the husbandman for?

positions.view: To supply the promise the address still lacked, comforting the disciples as the earlier part alarmed the scoffers.
To defend God's method of dealing with his people after a discourse of reproof.
To convict men who bring less wisdom to the signs of the times than to their own tillage.
To show that God does not always display his hand in one way, against the reading that makes it a reproach for ingratitude.
To rebuke scoffers who presume on long patience, since God has his times and seasons.
Fennel seed, on a modern identification, proverbial for its smallness.
Taken as they stand, one of the seeds sown and threshed by its own method.

outliers.note: Rejects the interpretation of the parable held by the Jewish expositors and the Greek and Latin commentators alike, that it reproaches the people for yielding no fruit.

themes: Give ye ear, and hear my voice; hearken, and hear my speech.
Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?
When he hath made plain the face thereof, doth he not cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cummin, and cast in the principal wheat and the appointed barley and the rie in their place?
For his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him.
For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod.
Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen.
This also cometh forth from the Lord of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working.
